newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ money market sells at close on profit taking.
newsitem.headline: NZ money market sells at close on profit taking.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
3-YR BONDS (DEC) UNTRADED 3-YR 7.22 (+9)
10-YR BONDS (DEC) UNTRADED 10-YR 7.20 (+4)
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.45 PCT (PREV 9.45) US 30-YR 6.70 (PREV 6.69)
* NZ debt market sells at close on profit taking
* Heavy trade on Futures and Options Exchange
* NZ$100 million 02/01 tender attracts reasonable interest
New Zealand 90-day bank bill rates broke up through nine percent at Thursday's close to end at 9.12 percent from their 8.97 percent open.
Dealers said there had been a good amount of profit-taking and solid offshore selling.
The 7/97s ended 18 points higher in yield, while the 7/98s were 12 points higher at 7.02 percent. Support was seen for the 90-days at 9.25 percent.

"I think a lot of the market was probably long, have stop-lossed out or taken profit and are just sitting here. A few of the guys have probably got a short position on here, and are just pushing it up, trying to find where the supports are coming in," a money market dealer said.
"One of the big concerns out there is the market is still fairly tight on cash, and a lot of this sell off was led by the perception that it was going to be higher," he added.

"That's also been shown in the forwards market, where there's no arbitrage opportunity between the forwards and the bills. Our bills market as a result has sold off quite aggressively, but we're still under the forwards."
Cash is currently at 9.45 percent, but spiked as high as 11 percent before the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said last week that monetary conditions were tighter than necessary.
Dealers saw 91.38 as a big support level for the December futures contracts, and said if it broke through that convincingly, to around 91.33 or 91.34, a strong sell off would result.

Bond dealers said the afternoon's tender of NZ$100 million February 2001 bonds went moderately well but with NZ$404 million in bids submitted (against NZ$662 million in the last tender) demand was not solid. One dealer said market expectations may have been a little high heading into the tender.

"It was an interesting one. The market was sitting around 7.22 percent in the 02/01s at the time, and people were probably a bit disappointed at the end of the day that it was a 19-mid," one dealer said.

"There also might have been a small amount of bonds that came onshore and saw the market sold, although I'm not completely convinced -- it almost felt as if it was being sold to be bought again," she added.

Friday's NAPM report and non-farm payrolls data in the U.S. was seen as the next major influence on the market. On the domestic front, markets were looking to the formation of the country's new government from ongoing coalition negotiations, which are likely to take weeks, and the Reserve Bank's next monetary policy statement on December 17.
